lessons.title: Inference, primitives, and literals
lessons.concept: TypeScript analyzes code without running it and builds a set of allowed values for every expression. const often preserves a precise literal, while let must accept future values compatible with its annotation or inference. explanation.title: Simple analogy
explanation.text: the most precise possible types is like a dimensioned blueprint that prevents incompatible parts from being assembled. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: string, number, and boolean describe broad sets; literals such as EUR | USD restrict a field to values understood by the domain. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

lessons.title: Generics, unknown, and type guards
lessons.concept: A generic represents a type not yet chosen but consistent across several positions, whereas unknown represents a value whose properties are not proven. A type guard connects a real JavaScript check to information TypeScript understands. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

explanation.text: validation of an untrusted value is like a dimensioned blueprint that prevents incompatible parts from being assembled. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

explanation.text: Result<T> preserves the exact data type in the ok branch and forbids reading data in the error branch; the generic describes this relationship without duplicating a type. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.
